newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus charges Russian journalists, Yeltsin angry.
newsitem.headline: Belarus charges Russian journalists, Yeltsin angry.

text.p: Belarus on Wednesday charged two Russian television journalists with illegally crossing its border with Lithuania, fuelling a bitter war of words with Moscow over their detention.
President Boris Yeltsin threatened to review a union treaty he signed with his authoritarian ex-Soviet neighbour Alexander Lukashenko just four months ago.

Pavel Sheremet, bureau chief for Russia's state-owned ORT network, his cameraman Dmitry Zavadsky and driver Yaroslav Ovchinnikov were detained by Belarussian border guards in the Belarus capital Minsk on Saturday and are now being held in the border town of Grodno.
ORT said the crew had some time earlier been filming a report in the border region.
Officials in the prosecutor's office said Sheremet and Zavadsky had been charged with an offence carrying up to five years in prison. Ovchinnikov has not been charged.
Sheremet was accused by the Belarussian authorities of biased reporting earlier this month and stripped of his foreign ministry media accreditation.
Earlier this year, Belarus expelled a reporter for Russia's NTV television.
Yeltsin, vacationing on the River Volga, said earlier on Wednesday he was "surprised and indignant" at the arrests and suggested Moscow might revise the union charter.

Lukashenko signed a charter with Yeltsin on a loose union between his country of 10 million and 150 million-strong Russia. The deal was watered down by Moscow liberals who feared it would give the hardline Lukashenko too much say in Kremlin policy.
One of the points in the union charter provided for the protection of press freedoms.

"Not a single country in the Commonwealth of Independent States has allowed itself anything of the sort Belarus has," Yeltsin said, referring to the grouping of former Soviet republics in remarks carried on ORT.
"I want Lukashenko to explain to me what is happening. Why don't we change the union charter if he doesn't like it?"
"We are not touching Belarus journalists, are we?" a visibly indignant Yeltsin said. "We have freedom."
Minsk did not hesitate to strike back.

"There is one law in Belarus for all citizens, including journalists," Russia's Interfax news agency quoted a senior aide to Lukashenko as saying. Under the union deal all Russians were granted Belarus citizenship and vice versa.
"ORT correspondents, who are also to some extent Belarussian citizens, cannot be seen as exceptions."
Despite the exchange of harsh words, both sides appeared keen to leave some room for manoeuvre.
"Much of this may be attributed to Lukashenko's lack of experience. I think we will work it out," Yeltsin said.
Lukashenko, a former collective farm manager, was a rank outsider when he won the 1994 presidential election.
Belrussian Foreign Minister Ivan Antonovich said he did not think the incident would seriously upset ties with Russia.

"Yes, Belarus hears what Russia is saying. But this incident cannot influence important joint policy," Antonovich told Reuters. "The two states have many common problems and Russia has many problems in which it needs Belarussian support."
Lukashenko defended the action against ORT journalists on Monday and accused the Russian media of waging war on him.
In the past, he has closed some newspapers down and ousted the editors of others. Some opposition newspapers are now published in Lithuania.
Lukashenko rewrote the constitution in November last year after a landslide win in a referendum which critics said was illegitimate. The new basic law gives him vast powers.
